knowledge: Neurodevelopmental disorder with progressive microcephaly, spasticity, and brain anomalies (NDMSBA, OMIM #617527) is an ultra-rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic loss-of-function or missense variants in PLAA (Phospholipase A2 Activating Protein), which encodes a protein involved in the ubiquitin-proteasome system and endosomal sorting. It was primarily delineated by Hall et al. (2017, PMID: 28414162) and corroborated by additional reports (e.g., Alazami et al., 2015, PMID: 25529582). Key core clinical characteristics include normal or borderline head circumference at birth followed by severe secondary/progressive microcephaly, profound global developmental delay / intellectual disability, early axial hypotonia rapidly progressing to spastic quadriplegia, seizures/epilepsy, optic atrophy, and distinct neuroimaging abnormalities including corpus callosum hypoplasia/thinning, delayed myelination, progressive cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, and sometimes white matter abnormalities.
prior_hypothesis: A patient with biallelic PLAA-related disorder can be clinically distinguished from other early-onset neurodegenerative and severe epileptic encephalopathies by the combination of normal head circumference at birth followed by rapidly evolving severe progressive microcephaly, profound axial hypotonia progressing to severe spasticity/hyperreflexia/contractures within the first 1-2 years of life, intractable seizures, optic atrophy, and characteristic neuroimaging showing progressive leukoencephalopathy, thin corpus callosum, and cerebellar/pontine volume loss. Phenotypic distinction purely from phenotype is challenging because it closely mimics CLN (neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis), pontocerebellar hypoplasias, and other ubiquitin-proteasome disorders (e.g., UFM1 pathway or PEHO-like syndromes), making molecular genetic confirmation necessary.

candidate_answers.answer: In the index discovery cohort (Hall et al., 2017, PMID: 28414162), progressive microcephaly (HP:0000253) was present in approximately 100% (e.g., 6/6 or all assessable affected individuals in the primary multiplex families), often with normal or near-normal occipitofrontal circumference at birth followed by drops to below -3 to -4 SD.

Severe developmental delay / intellectual disability (HP:0001263 / HP:0001249) and early hypotonia progressing to spasticity/spastic tetraparesis (HP:0001284 / HP:0002510) are present in virtually 100% of reported individuals (e.g., Hall et al., 2017, PMID: 28414162).
candidate_answers.aspect: Core motor and developmental phenotype frequencies

candidate_answers.answer: Neuroimaging hallmarks include corpus callosum hypoplasia/thinning (HP:0002079), progressive cerebral atrophy (HP:0002059), cerebellar atrophy (HP:0001272), and delayed/defective myelination (HP:0002187), seen in nearly all affected patients with serial MRI scans.

The most discriminating clinical features that separate PLAA-related disorder from primary microcephalies (e.g., MCPH) are the postnatal/progressive nature of the microcephaly accompanied by neurodegenerative features (spasticity, seizures, optic atrophy, brain atrophy) rather than stable congenital microcephaly with isolated intellectual disability.

The condition can be distinguished from typical pontocerebellar hypoplasia (PCH) or classical leukodystrophies by normal prenatal/birth imaging and head size, absence of classic dragonfly/butterfly cerebellar patterns on neonatal MRI, and specific endosomal/lysosomal storage markers being negative.
candidate_answers.aspect: Differential diagnosis versus PCH and storage diseases

candidate_answers.answer: Major congenital structural malformations outside the central nervous system (e.g., congenital heart disease, renal anomalies, skeletal dysplasia, limb reduction defects) are typically absent, and their presence strongly argues against isolated PLAA deficiency.

There is no known sex predilection or significant sex-dependent phenotypic divergence, as PLAA is autosomal (chromosome 9p21); both homozygous and compound heterozygous loss-of-function or missense variants result in a consistently severe neurodevelopmental regression/arrest phenotype.

assumptions: The scope is strictly restricted to biallelic germline alterations in PLAA causing OMIM #617527.

A reliable clinical diagnosis from phenotype alone must rely on specific combinations of neuroimaging, neuro-ophthalmological, and developmental trajectories, while acknowledging that genetic testing is standard of care for definitive diagnosis.
Reported cohorts are very small due to the ultra-rare nature of the condition (likely <20 total published cases globally).
